passage: Monday. Kamal said, "The track is the shortcut to the mango grove. Come on." Irfan's feet were ready, but his mind asked: what if a train comes and there is no room to step aside? What if my foot slips between the sleepers? He had no good answer to either. Tuesday. Irfan said, "I will not walk on the track. If you like, we go by the road." Kamal grumbled but went by the road with him. Wednesday. At dinner Irfan told his father about the shortcut, and his father phoned Kamal's family to say the track is no place for children. Kamal did not speak to Irfan that day, but on Thursday he came with mangoes.

qa.q: What two questions did Irfan ask himself about the railway track?
qa.a: He asked what if a train comes and there is no room to step aside, and what if his foot slips between the sleepers.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling on Monday when Kamal called the track a shortcut?
qa.a: Uneasy and cautious, since his feet were ready but his mind was troubled by questions he could not answer.

qa.q: What could Irfan do if friends keep pressing him about the track?
qa.a: Tell an adult such as his father, because a grown-up can stop the danger.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel about Irfan's father phoning his family?
qa.a: Embarrassed and annoyed at first, which fits not speaking to Irfan that day, though he came back with mangoes on Thursday.

grounding: Before agreeing to walk on the railway track, a boy asks what could go wrong, and the answers settle the choice.

subtype: Approach: predicting what could go wrong [Thinking]
passage: Jasleen, puttar, sit. Your Kishore Nanu wasn't always this slow old man. When I was ten, the boys of our mohalla dared me to walk the railway line from the level crossing to the signal post, balancing on one rail. Bittu said it was easy. I stood there with one foot on the steel and asked him, "And if a train comes round the bend?" He said, "You jump off." "And if my foot slips and gets stuck between the sleepers?" He didn't answer that. Nobody did. That silence decided it for me. I took my foot off the rail and went home for lunch. Two of them went anyway, and the gateman chased them off, waving his flag and shouting.

qa.q: Where was the railway walk meant to start and end?
qa.a: It was meant to go from the level crossing to the signal post.

qa.q: What was young Kishore feeling as he stood with one foot on the rail?
qa.a: He was probably nervous and unsure, wanting to fit in with the boys but worried enough to ask what could go wrong.

qa.q: What turned the choice for young Kishore, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking his "what if" questions out loud: when nobody could answer about a foot stuck between the sleepers, the danger was plain and he could leave without a long argument.

qa.q: How might Bittu have felt when Kishore asked about his foot slipping?
qa.a: Bittu may have felt caught out and uneasy, because he had no answer and the dare suddenly looked much less easy than he had claimed.

grounding: An elder recalls asking what could go wrong before a railway-track dare and letting the answers decide.

passage: The fair closed at seven, and it was already ten to. "The track is quickest," said Kashish, stepping onto the gravel. "Unless you're too scared to walk it." Fog hung so thick that Sahil could barely see the first signal light. He stopped at the edge. "If a train comes, could we even see it in this?" Kashish shrugged. "We'd hear it." "Over the loudspeakers from the fair? And if my foot slips on a wet sleeper?" She went quiet. Sahil turned back toward the road. "Road's longer. Maybe we miss the fair. That's all we'd miss." They got there as the last stalls were rolling down their shutters, and shared the one paper cone of roasted peanuts still for sale.

qa.q: What time did the fair close?
What might Sahil have been worried about as he stood at the edge of the gravel?
qa.a: He was worried and uneasy that the fog and the fair's loudspeakers would hide a train, and that his foot could slip on a wet sleeper.

qa.q: What else could Sahil have done if Kashish had stepped onto the track anyway?
qa.a: He could refuse to follow and tell the nearest adult straight away, because an adult can stop someone near a track in a way a cousin or friend can't.

qa.q: Why might Kashish have gone quiet?
qa.a: She may have felt unsure once Sahil's questions showed dangers she hadn't thought about, especially in the fog.

grounding: Shows a child asking what happens if a train comes or a foot slips, and the answers making the choice clear under time pressure.
